parties:
Rahela Khatun ----- Petitioner.
Vs.
Chairman, Court of Settlement, Bangladesh Abandoned Buildings, Segunbagicha, Ramna, Dhaka and ors. ----- Respondents.
full_judgment:
Md. Abdul Jalil J: This Rule calls in question a judgment and order dated 23.2.89 passed by the Court of Settlement in Case No. 1043 of 1987. 

 2. The petitioner's case is that she filed a case, under section 7 of the Abandoned Buildings (Supplementary Provisions) Ordinance, 1985(Ordinance No. LIV of 1985) praying for exclusion of Holding No. 2/10, Block-F, Joint Quarter, Mohammadpur, (Kha-20) from the 'Kha' list of abandoned buildings published on 23.9.86 in Bangladesh. Gazette (Extraordinary) contending that the said holding was allotted to one Qumrul Hoque, an immigrant from India as a lessee by the Government and possession was delivered to him on 4.2.63. The said Qumrul Hoque executed a bainapatra in favour of Mosammat Rahela Khatun, the petitioner, on 20.11.70 agreeing to sell the said holding to her at a consideration of Tk. 8,000.00 on receipt of Tk. 6,500.00 as earnest money and thereafter the petitioner paid further amount of Tk. 1000.00 later on and there was a balance of Tk. 500.00 only to be paid at the time of registration of the kabala as per terms of the contract. The said vendor having failed to execute and register the necessary Deed, the petitioner filed. Title Suit No. 67 of 1975 against said Qumrul Hoque and obtained a decree for specific performance of contract and in execution of the said decree obtained a kabala through court on 25.9.79 and thereby the petitioner became the absolute owner of the said holding. In the said suit the Secretary, Ministry of Works and the Government of Bangladesh, represented by the Deputy Commissioner, Dhaka were added as defendants, but none contested the suit. The Government filed Miscellaneous Case No. 217 of 1986 in the 2nd Court of Subordinate Judge, Dhaka for setting aside the said ex parte decree under Order 9, rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure which was also dismissed for default. Thereafter the said holding was included in the 'Kha' list of the abandoned buildings on 23.9.86 published in the Bangladesh Gazette and, as such, the petitioner had to file the said case. 

 3. The respondent-Government did not file any written statement but contested the case by way of making verbal submissions contending that the whereabouts of the petitioner's vendor were not known and he left the house uncared and, as such, it vested in the Government under President's Order No. 16 of 1972 and was allotted to one Mariam Begum on 1.4.72 and that the petitioner's Bainapatra is a concocted one executed by fictitious person other that the lessee and the transfer through Court is the outcome of the fraudulent decree and is void ab initio. 

 4. The Court of Settlement after hearing dismissed the case by the impugned judgment and order dated 23.2.89 as aforesaid. 

 5. Being aggrieved by the said order, the petitioner filed an application under Article 102 of the Constitution in this Court on which the aforesaid Rule was issued calling upon the respondents, namely, the Chairman, Court of Settlement and the Secretary, Ministry of Works to show cause why the said judgment and order passed by the Settlement Court, Dhaka on 23.2.89 in case No. 1043 of 1987 should not be declared to have been made without lawful authority and of no legal effect. 

 8. Mr. Quazi Akhtar Hossain, the learned Assistant Attorney-General appearing for the respondent No. 2, on the other hand, submits that the alleged agreement although executed in 1970 was not acted upon till the suit was filed and the petitioner did not acquire any title before the decree and, as such, in 1972 Qumrul Hoque remained the owner and he having left the place, it was rightly taken over as an abandoned property and still continuing as abandoned property and all subsequent acts are void as no suit lies touching an abandoned property. He further submits that the learned Court of Settlement acted with lawful authority in rejecting the case. 

 11. The learned Court of Settlement came to the finding that the bainapatra was executed by a fictitious person other than the lessee and that the lessee was absent possibly because he left the country as alleged by the Government and the petitioner could not establish the whereabouts and presence of the lessee and, as such, the holding fell within the mischief of Article 2 of President's Order No. 16 of 1972. It was further held that the transfer is subject to Articles 6, 14(1) of President's Order No. 16 of 1972 read with section 44 of the Evidence Act and Article 5(2) of Ordinance No. 54 of 1985. 

 12. We have already observed that on the basis of the agreement dated 30.11.70 a decree for specific performance of contract was passed and in execution of the decree a deed of sale was executed and registered and the Government was a party to that suit. Hence, the said decree is binding on the Government unless and until the said decree is set aside or declared void by any court of competent jurisdiction. A party to the suit cannot say that an agreement is forged which was the basis of the decree. The Court of Settlement has no power to set aside a decree of the Civil Court but it has the jurisdiction only to decide the matter on the basis of the papers produced and so the decree stands against the Government. It further appeared that the Government filed a case under Order, 9, rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure for setting aside the said ex parte decree but it was rejected. 

 15. Be that as it may, without entering into the disputed question of facts, it may be said that even not a scrap of paper showing that the said property was taken over as an abandoned property was produced by the Government either before the Court of Settlement or in this Court, It is the case of the petitioner that by virtue of the agreement he has been in possession of the same. However, we have already observed that we are not going to enter into the disputed question of facts as to whether the petitioner or the Government is in possession of the holding in question. 

 17. So, this section goes against the respondents as the petitioner produced a judgment and decree. The burden is on the adverse party, namely, the Government in this case, to show that the Court was not competent to pass the decree. 

 18. In the facts and circumstances as discussed above, we are of the opinion that the learned Court of Settlement acted without lawful authority in dismissing the case. 

 In the result, the Rule is made absolute without, however, any order as to costs and the judgment and order dated 23.2.89 passed by the Court of Settlement in case No. 1043 of 1987 as evidenced by Annexure Ito the petition is declared to have been made without any lawful authority.
